review_text:
Does the trick and more. I bought these because I was taking my wife and daughter on a long trip from Honolulu to Washington D.C. and wanted to add as much comfort as I could to the flights. Actually, I first bought a pair of sale-priced Maxell NC-II headphones to see what the noise-cancellation was like and whether it was worth it. Yep, it did seem like it would make a difference. There were three of us, so I needed two more. Researching the different models available, I became very curious how much better the more expensive models were, so what I did was buy another sale-priced Maxell, and then succumbed to my curiosity for the third. I figured it might be nice to have a better headphone for home use too. My research pointed at three price levels for noise-canceling headphones, with the Bose at the top, a variety around the $100 price range, and the lower price range with the Maxell and a Sony I found in the stores. The Sony was definitely out of the question because they were not the cup design that covered the complete ear. I wanted to spend money on the lower range of the mid-priced models, and I narrowed it down to either these Jabra C820S or the Logitech Noise Canceling model. The Logitech were cheaper than the Jabra by an amount significant enough that I was close to buying them instead. Reviewers seemed mostly pleased with the Logitech's sound quality. The raves were about equal to the Jabra on that issue. There was one factor that made me go for the more expensive Jabra. Many of the reviewers for the Logitech model complained that the Logitech model could easily break at the swivel joint, and some complained that they even arrived in the package already broken, so why risk that, I thought.

I'm very happy with the Jabras. They do the trick quite nicely. The noise cancellation is noticeably better than the Maxells. I let my daughter use the Jabras on the plane and she fell asleep with them easily. The detachable cord is a significant factor to consider. Fall asleep on the plane, roll over in the wrong way, and you could be putting a strong tug on that cord. Even more so, I used the Jabras while I was on a treadmill at the hotel, and many times my swinging hand came down and knocked the cord right out of its connection to the phones. For what we wanted in the airplane situation, the Maxells worked fine for me and my wife, despite not having detachable cords, but I doubt I'll ever be using them at home. The Jabras have good enough fidelity when the noise canceling feature is on that they also make nice phones for personal stereophonics. With the noise canceling off, the fidelity drops significantly, but you know, so what? If you want to listen to music, you're better off with the outside noises canceled anyway. A true audiophile might complain about a slight hiss from the noise cancellation feature, but it's not noticeable for me.

The case the Jabras come with is nice and sturdy. It's a little nuts in the way it can completely zip apart. I can't think of why they designed it that way. If you zip it completely apart, its a little tedious putting the zipper back together, but if you're conscious of what you're doing, you'll remember not to unzip the whole way. The truth is, though, the Maxells fold up nicer into a smaller ball which I prefer--makes it fast to put them away when you're through with them. The Jabras, though, are definitely a much better headphone. Now I've got one decent set of headphones connected to my computer, and two sets of Maxells in storage waiting to accompany them on our next trip.

Note: At the time I bought these, the Logitechs were everywhere selling cheaper. Right now they're significantly more expensive than the Jabras on Amazon. There are such huge differences in list prices and street prices on these things and prices fluctuate often. Buyer beware.
